item.title: 伊朗安全负责人威胁邻国反对经济措施和其他中东事态发展
item.description:
The new leader of Iran’s top security body is threatening neighbors against joining new U.S. efforts to squeeze Tehran’s economy. Egypt is trying to revive Iran-U.S. negotiations. And Iraq and Iran say Tehran has helped some ships carrying Iraqi oil to transit theStrait of Hormuz. France and Saudi Arabia are expected to discuss plans to bypass the waterway.
Meanwhile, Israel has carried out strikes in Syria and in Gaza.
Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Saturday. Full coverage can befound here.
The hard-line new leader of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council threatened Tehran’s neighbors against joining the new U.S. effort to hurt Iran’s economy, and accused the United States of increasing global nuclear insecurity with months of war.
“If (Trump) wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” he said in an interview with the state broadcaster that aired Saturday.
Mohsen Rezaei was named this month as part of senior appointments widely seen as hardening Tehran’s political and military stance. His interview with IRIB is his most extensive public statement since then.
Rezaei said Iran would target oil-shipping routes out of the Persian Gulf — alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz — if neighbors join what he described as the economic war against Iran. Those neighbors would be considered enemies and “we will target their interests,” he said.
U.S. President Donald Trump in the past week has vowed to increase Iran’s pain by imposing an “unprecedented” level of economic warfare and isolation. Iran has lived under sanctions for years.
Rezaei said discussions with Oman, located on the other side of the strait, over management of it were ongoing, and said fees would be imposed. Iran asserted control over what was seen as an international waterway shortly after the U.S. and Israel attacked on Feb. 28.
Rezaei also vowed to make changes to Iran’s diplomacy and bring new capabilities to what he called the next war. He warned the U.S. against sending more military personnel to the region, and said the U.S. had increased nuclear insecurity because countries see that participating in international monitoring efforts, as Iran has done, is no protection against attack.
The top diplomats for Egypt and Iran discussed efforts to bring Tehran and Washington back to the negotiating table to settle the war, Egypt’s foreign ministry said.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Egyptian counterpart Badr Abdelatty also discussed the Iranian-Omani talks, the ministry said.
Araghchi briefed Egypt’s foreign minister about “Iran’s view of ongoing developments, the course of negotiations and their challenges,” the ministry said, without elaborating. Araghchi confirmed the call. Separately, Araghchi said he had a call with Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir,
Residents swim as cargo and commercial vessels are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA via AP)
The governments of Iraq and Iran said Tehran has helped some ships carrying Iraqi oil to transit the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for global oil, natural gas and other supplies, but there were few details.
“There is facilitation for some ships carrying Iraqi oil in the Strait of Hormuz,” Iraqi President Nizar Amidi said in comments published Saturday by the state-run news agency, adding that Iraq doesn’t have a national carrier for transporting oil.
Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency said a number of Iraqi oil tankers have been permitted to transit. It was not clear how many or what Iran might have received in return.
An Israeli drone strike on a vehicle wounded one person on Saturday in the southwestern Syrian village of Beit Jin, according to the Syrian state news agency SANA. Syria’s foreign ministry said several civilians were injured and called the strike a flagrant violation of the country’s sovereignty.
The Israeli military said it targeted a “terrorist who advanced terror attacks in final stages of preparation,” without elaborating. It wasn’t immediately clear if it was the same strike.
Israel has carried out hundreds of airstrikes around Syria after the ouster of former President Bashar Assad in late 2024, mainly destroying army assets to keep them out of the hands of his successors.
In an interview on Friday with Mario Nawfal, a Lebanese-Australian entrepreneur,U.S. Ambassador Tom Barracksaid Israel “still” occupies the Golan Heights in violation of U.N. resolutions.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Saturday in a statement called Barrack’s remarks “full of inaccuracies and positions that contradict Trump’s own position.”
Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 war and annexed it in 1981. The U.N. considers the territory occupied Syrian land. But in March 2019, Trump signed a proclamation recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, reversing decades of U.S. policy.
French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman are expected to discuss plans to develop alternatives routes to the Strait of Hormuz during the Saudi leader’s two-day visit to Paris that starts on Sunday, according to officials in the presidency who weren’t authorized to be publicly named.
Proposals include increasing trade through Omani ports outside of the Persian Gulf, expanding or doubling pipelines in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere, and developing new rail links, the officials said.
France and Saudi Arabia have formed a task force on energy and logistics connections between the Middle East and Europe that is scheduled to meet at the ministerial level Monday. The officials said the work would focus on identifying the most strategic projects, securing financing and establishing roles for French companies.
— AP correspondent Angela Charlton in Paris
The Israeli army demolishes buildings east of Deir al-Balah, central Gaza Strip, Saturday Aug. 22, 2026. (AP Photo/Abdel Kareem Hana)
An Israeli strike on the backyard of a house in centralGazakilled one Palestinian and wounded another Saturday, according to health officials at Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital.
Israel’s military said it targeted Sharif al-Hasanat, a Hamas commander who “advanced terror attacks and took part in efforts to restore Hamas’ underground infrastructure.” Days earlier, a U.S. negotiatorreportedly asked Israelto draw down attacks while seeking to make progress on the ceasefire.

item.title: 野火暴露并引爆了第一次世界大战和第二次世界大战中埋藏的炸弹和地雷
item.description:
ELSENBORN, Belgium (AP) — The wildfiresburning across Europe this summerhave exposed a potentially deadly threat lurking beneath the blackened landscape: rustybombs and minesfrom World War I and II that threaten crews responding to the flames.
Some of the weapons have exploded in the intense heat. Blasts have been reported in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, where a bomb-disposal team was dispatched to check a forest threatened by flames neara site of fierce fightingin the Limburg province in 1944.
Smoke rises from a field scorched by a wildfire near Waimes, Belgium, Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo AP/Marius Burgelman, File)
Fueled by climate change, the fires and explosions show that the continent’s “climatic luck” is running out, said Sarah Njeri, a peace and conflict scholar at London’s School of Oriental and African Studies. Steady temperatures and predictable rainfall once ensured that most buried weapons stayed dormant.
“Climate change is now doing the work of unburying and reactivating what was previously stable,” Njeri said. Fires can ignite old munitions but can also burn away the scrub and brush that hides them.
This wildfire seasonwas superchargedby heavy rains in January that spurred vegetation growth, which became kindling when the summer heat arrived. Those temperatures, combined with drought conditions, low humidity and stiff winds, offered an ideal environment for fire, according to a study issued last month by the World Weather Attribution group.
As they advanced, the flames moved over territory that has long been known to hold unexploded weapons, a lethal legacy that lingered long after the guns fell silent.
In a forest in tinder-dry France, a massive wildfire outside the southwestern city of Bordeaux uncovered a cache of what is believed to be World War II-era ammunition.
In the eastern Belgian province of Liege, Gov. Hervé Jamar said “a few sporadic detonations” were recently heard and that emergency services were adapting to account for munitions buried in a fire area. He said no fire crews were in danger, but local media published photos of a firefighter handling a rusted bomb.
During World War II, booby traps, bombs and mines were sprinkled throughout the province’s dense peat-bog forest known as the High Fens. In the first four years after Germany’s surrender in 1945, the munitions killed six civilians, said Bernard Collard, a local historian who runs the Truschbaum Museum near Belgium’s border with Germany that houses a collection of found objects from the war.
Bernard Collard runs a metal detector over a field in the Elsenborn area of Krinkelt, Belgium, Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. (AP Photo/Valentin Bianchi)
“When you go into a forest like this, you are not sure where the explosives are,” he said. He remembers his father detonating a found bomb in a quarry.
The fire in the High Fens, which stretches across the border with Germany, is smoldering atop a much-bloodied battlefield where Nazis fought Allied troops. The Battle of the Bulge was fought in and around the High Fens.
The fire is even closer to the sites of two lesser-known skirmishes along Elsenborn Ridge and in the Hurtgen Forest, which lasted 88 days and killed about 33,000 American and 28,000 German troops.
World War I shells, some marked in pink are suspect gas shells, are piled in a warehouse at the explosive disposal facility (DOVO) in Poelkapelle, Belgium, April 21, 2015. (AP Photo/Geert Vanden Wijngaert, File)
Collard is authorized to scan with a metal detector the former battlefields, now forests, pastures and farmland. He has found mortar shells, machine guns, helmets, cigarette cases, and once, a human skeleton.
“You never know what you might come across, and you shouldn’t take it lightly,” Collard said while standing in a field that was once a blood-soaked site. Nearby, blueberry bushes cover old foxholes, trenches and deep craters from artillery fire.
He frequently works with the Belgian demining squad. “It’s part of our history. We live with it,” Collard said.
Unexploded ordnance is even more dangerous around wildfires because heat can trigger the explosives, said Jonas Tepe, a spokesperson for North Rhine-Westphalia, just across the border in Germany.
The Belgian Ministry of Defense said it receives requests from the region about every week to assist in disarming explosives, yet it does not consider the area a “hot spot” compared to elsewhere in Belgium. Such requests are even more common in the west, where farmers in towns such as Ypres — infamous for harrowing trench warfare in World War I — call the annual tilling of the soil “the iron harvest” because it turns up so many war remnants.
Every year across the nation, Belgium’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Destruction Service responds to more than 3,000 calls and disposes of 200 to 250 tons of munitions left over from both world wars.
Charlotte Cardoen-Descamps points out different types of World War I shells that were found on her farm in Poelkapelle, Belgium, May 4, 2007, in what is known as the “iron harvest”. (AP Photo/Virginia Mayo, File)
Drought has also helped to lay the past bare by shrinking rivers and lakes to reveal old weapons.
In Slovakia, the Danube River fell and exposed two naval mines that police pulled out of the water and buried in a trench for a controlled demolition. Authorities in Hungary closed Budapest’s Margaret Bridge aftera bomb dating from World War II emergedat its base in receding water.
As the Rhine dried up, Germanauthorities also found a WWII-era bomb.
Christina Greene, a researcher at the University of Arizona who, with Njeri, wrotean articleon Europe’s wildfires and unexploded ordnance risk, said “the legacy of war keeps creeping up” because of climate change.
“It’s reliving the legacies of war and conflict in a way that we haven’t had to deal with in a while in certain places.”
___ Associated Press writers Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands; Sylvain Plazy in Brussels; Angela Charlton in Paris; Kirsten Grieshaber in Berlin; and Stanislav Hodina in Prague contributed to this report.

item.title: 加拿大和美国之间的贸易战进一步破裂了曾经紧密而持久的联盟
item.description:
TORONTO (AP) — For decades, Canada built much of its prosperity on privileged access to the United States. Now,after the collapse of trade talks, one of the world’s closest and most durable alliances has been fundamentally altered, with both countries facing the risk of afull-scale trade war.
Prime Minister Mark Carney acknowledged the break after last-ditch negotiations failed Friday, saying Canada had recognized that “America has changed” and that the countries would “not return to our old relationship.”
The United States imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods early Saturday. Carney said Canada would retaliate dollar for dollar beginning Sept. 8, targeting sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.
Carney foreshadowed the shiftat theWorld Economic Forumin Davos in January, declaring that the world was experiencing “a rupture, not a transition” and urging countries such as Canada to reduce their vulnerability to economic coercion by strengthening their economies at home and diversifying abroad.
He said in Ottawa on Saturday that warning had been borne out. He accused the U.S. of using “economic integration as a weapon” and said its “signature was written in pencil.”
“The collapse of the tariff talks points to the fact that the old Canada-U.S. relationship is over and, for many Canadians, it also confirms the perception that Canada can’t trust the Trump administration,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
The pressure from Republican President Donald Trump has gone well beyond tariffs.
He has questionedCanada’s economic viability, repeatedly talked about making itthe 51st U.S. stateand used trade measures to encourage production to move from Canada to the United States. That has angered many Canadians and fueled a sense of betrayal in a country that had long regarded the U.S. as its closest ally.
Canadian travel to the U.S. remains sharply lower than before the dispute, with July return trips down nearly 29% by car and 27% by air from July 2024, Statistics Canada said.
The failed negotiations underscored how far the relationship had shifted. Canada had been prepared to accept some U.S. tariffs for market access and greater certainty — a break from decades of policy aimed at eliminating trade barriers.
For Canadians accustomed to preferential access under the 1989 Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, NAFTA and its successor, even reduced tariffs would mark a retreat from the old relationship.
The collapse also puts Carney’s approach to Trump to the test.
The prime minister’s “elbows up” posture — hockey shorthand for playing aggressively and refusing to be pushed around — has helped keep him popular at home. His decision to resist U.S. pressure could also resonate abroad with those impressed by his Davos call for countries to resist economic coercion and reduce dependence on great powers.
Provincial and conservative leaders broadly backed Carney. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said “the old status quo is not possible,” while Ontario Premier Doug Ford praised Carney for rejecting what he called a bad deal for the auto, steel and manufacturing sectors.
Ford said Trump “is not to be trusted whatsoever.”
Former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney said Canada was “not cravenly surrendering in the face of constant economic and political aggression.”
Lana Payne, national president of Unifor, Canada’s largest private-sector union, accused Trump of trying to weaken Canada’s industrial base.
“What we have seen from the U.S. administration, or Donald Trump, is this consistent attempt to try and destroy the industrial economy of Canada with tariffs that have been strategically designed to attack us,” Payne said.
Nearly three-quarters of Canada’s goods exports go to the United States. The U.S. economy is roughly 10 times larger than Canada’s, limiting Ottawa’s ability to retaliate dollar for dollar without inflicting disproportionate damage at home.
Royal Bank of Canada economists estimate the tariffs directly affect about 0.4% of Canada’s GDP because they cover only about 5% of Canadian exports to the U.S. The damage could grow if retaliation broadens, more sectors are targeted or the dispute curbs investment and disrupts supply chains.
Carney himself acknowledged the cost of retaliation, saying the Canadian measures would “raise costs and reduce choice for Canadians.” He said his government would announce additional assistance for affected businesses and workers.
Béland said the countries were witnessing “the beginning of a full-scale trade war,” though he cautioned that the situation could change rapidly.
Carney said Canada supplies 99% of U.S. natural gas imports, 85% of its electricity imports and 60% of its crude oil imports. Trump has focused much of his pressure on autos, steel and aluminum, fueling resentment among Canadians who see the push as an effort to hollow out key industries.
Goldy Hyder, president and CEO of the Business Council of Canada, said businesses still view the U.S. as Canada’s most important trading partner but increasingly see the shift as lasting beyond Trump.
“There is a new trade and investment model, one that could well be kept in place by future U.S. administrations whether Democrat or Republican,” Hyder said.
The breakdown adds urgency to Carney’s push to diversify beyond the United States. He has traveled abroad seeking investment and new trade ties, aiming to attract $1 trillion Canadian (US$730 billion) by 2030 and double non-U.S. investment over the next decade. Canada has signed more than 20 trade and security agreements across five continents in the past year.
That made Washington’s effort to restrict Canada’s ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries particularly significant.
In July, Ottawa and Alberta advanced plans for a new Pacific Coast oil pipeline to give Canadian crude greater access to Asian markets and reduce reliance on U.S. buyers.
The immediate question is how long the latest tariff confrontation will last.
Béland said the deeper change probably will, partly because U.S. protectionism is likely to remain influential under future administrations.
“The idea that things will return to ‘normal’ once Donald Trump leaves the White House is probably just wishful thinking,” Béland said. “It doesn’t mean the relationship might not improve in the future but that things will never be the same.”

item.title: 联邦法官撤销特朗普暂停处理 75 个国家移民签证的政策
item.description:
纽约一名联邦法官撤销了特朗普政府暂停处理来自 75 个国家签证的政策，其中包括阿富汗、伊朗、俄罗斯和索马里，特朗普政府认为这些国家的国民可能需要在美国提供公共援助。
前总统乔·拜登任命的美国地区法官珍妮特·巴尔加斯周五撤销了这项政策，称其“违反法律且超出法定权力”。
法官裁定，国务卿马可·卢比奥发布这项政策超越了他的职权，该政策要求“在没有任何法律依据的情况下拒绝向符合条件的申请人发放签证”，从而“违反”了《移民和国籍法》。
巴尔加斯表示，这项政策还破坏了国会将领事官员置于任何签证决定最前线的要求。
她写道：“国会赋予这些官员专属权力和自由裁量权，根据对法规中规定的具体和详细标准的审查来确定移民是否有资格获得签证。”“该政策明确禁止根据申请人的国籍签发移民签证，代表着对这一法定计划的直接废除。”
该政策受到两个非营利组织以及 11 个人的质疑，其中 6 人的家庭成员被拒绝签证。其余五人在国外，并已提交“基于就业的申请”来美国。
“我们欢迎这一裁决，因为从本质上讲，此案是为了让家庭团聚，”CLICNIC 的执行董事安娜·加拉格尔 (Anna Gallagher) 说。CLICNIC 是一家全国性非营利组织，为移民法律服务提供商网络提供培训、资源和支持，也是原告之一。
她在一份声明中说：“天主教的社会教义要求我们维护每个人的尊严，并承认家庭是社会的基础。”“这一决定肯定了这些价值观和法治，让家庭再次朝着团聚迈进。”
另一原告是位于哈莱姆区的非营利组织非洲社区。其一位领导人称这一裁决是“法治的巨大胜利”。
负责政策和宣传的副执行主任戴安娜·科纳特在一份声明中表示：“这项非法的种族主义禁令造成了不可估量的伤害，残酷地使家人和亲人分离。”“今天，我们很高兴地告诉我们的社区成员：这项禁令已不再存在。”
唐纳德·特朗普总统实施了越来越多的移民和旅行禁令，主要针对来自非洲、亚洲和拉丁美洲的人。美国国务院周六表示，特朗普政府正在“通过维护签证申请人的最高筛选和审查标准来保护美国人民”，并且不会对未决诉讼发表评论。
该政策发布时，国务院表示已指示领事官员停止来自 75 个国家的移民签证申请，这是根据 11 月份一项更广泛的命令，该命令收紧了对可能成为“公共负担”的潜在移民的规定。美国国务院根据经济顾问委员会的数据表示，超过 30% 的来自这些国家的移民家庭获得了某种形式的公共援助。
发给所有美国大使馆和领事馆的另一份通知称，非移民签证申请人也应接受“全面审查和筛选”，以确定他们可能在美国寻求公共福利的可能性。
美联社获得了该电报的副本，电报多次指出，申请人必须证明他们在美国期间不会申请公共福利，而怀疑申请人可能申请的领事官员应要求他们填写一份表格，证明其财务真实性。
该裁决是法院颠覆特朗普移民议程的最新例子。六月，一名联邦法官推翻了特朗普政府的一项政策，该政策使来自数十个国家的移民更难进入和留在美国，影响到庇护、工作许可、绿卡和公民身份申请等要素。该法官表示，这项政策使无数移民的生活“陷入不确定的法律困境”，并指责美国公民和移民服务局无视法律。

item.title: 包船捕捞 1,260 磅重的蓝马林鱼，据信是东海岸最大的捕获量
item.description:
缅因州波特兰（美联社）——达蒙·萨科（Damon Sacco）从未见过像他和其他钓鱼者在马萨诸塞州附近水域搏斗了几个小时的鱼一样的东西。当它从深处升起时，看起来就像一艘闪烁着蓝色光芒的飞船。
萨科是马萨诸塞州的一名长期包租渔船船长，他看到巨大的鱼鳍浮出水面，起初他以为自己面对的是一条巨大的鲨鱼。
“然后我仔细观察了一下，我想，天哪，那东西很尖锐，”他说。“但这对马林鱼来说太大了。”
他错了。萨科和他的客户沃尔特·查普曼周三在美国东海岸捕获了他们和其他人认为是有史以来最大的大西洋蓝枪鱼。这条巨大的长嘴鱼长度超过 11 英尺（335 厘米），当他们将其带回马萨诸塞州法尔茅斯的陆地时，其重量为 1,260 磅（571.5 公斤）。
根据国际钓鱼协会保存的记录，这一重量仅比 1992 年在巴西海域捕获的大西洋蓝马林鱼的世界纪录低 142 磅（64.4 公斤）。
缅因大学远洋渔业实验室主任、该大学海洋科学学院副教授沃尔特·戈莱特表示，在新英格兰海域捕获如此巨大的鱼可能更加了不起。东北地区一年中大部分时间水温太冷，捕捉大鱼的机会非常狭窄。
Golet 表示，这条鱼的头部正在运往缅因大学实验室，以确定它的年龄，他推测它的年龄可能在 25 到 30 年之间。
他说：“我不认为大西洋捕获的蓝马林鱼数量在未来几年内会达到 1,200 磅以上。”
捕捞当天，萨科的包租船卡斯塔法里 (Castafari) 正在亚特兰蒂斯峡谷捕鱼，亚特兰蒂斯峡谷是位于大陆架边缘的水下峡谷，距科德角约 100 英里（160 公里）。戈莱特说，高度洄游的蓝马林鱼是该地区的季节性游客。
与马林鱼的战斗持续了大约三个小时，查普曼用鱼竿和卷线器进行了战斗。萨科说，他在冒险的大部分时间里扮演的角色是“开着巴士到处转，并对人们大喊大叫”。他补充说，这条鱼在船的横梁和喙上留下了几个洞，他认为这是“战争痕迹”。
来自普利茅斯的退休人员查普曼一生都是渔民，他说鱼肉被大约十几个人分了，他目前正在寻找如何处理鱼的食谱。他说，马林鱼无疑是他钓过的最大的鱼，其中一些可能会被用来做鱼杂烩。
“我不会一个人吃掉 1,200 磅重的鱼，”查普曼说。
当船返回码头时，一群人正在等待，称鱼的重量成了一个短暂的景象。法尔茅斯的旁观者凯蒂·柯兰 (Katie Curran) 表示，这真是太壮观了。
柯兰说：“人们一生都在捕鱼，却从未有过这样的收获。”“向达蒙·萨科船长和船员们致敬，他们收获了一生难忘的收获。”

item.title: 随着风力增强，热带风暴莫克向夏威夷推进
item.description:
火奴鲁鲁（美联社）——热带风暴莫克周六向夏威夷推进，可能给大岛带来更多强降雨和强阵风，当地居民仍在应对飓风拉拉造成的严重洪水和破坏性大风的后果。
2026 年 8 月 17 日星期一，飓风拉拉带来大雨后，夏威夷纳阿莱胡的一条道路被泥土冲毁。（艾娜·阿卡姆，美联社）
莫克于周五在太平洋形成，位于希洛东南约 425 英里（680 公里）处，以 12 英里/小时（19 公里/小时）的速度向西北偏西移动。国家飓风中心表示，最大持续风速约为 50 英里/小时（85 公里/小时）。
与飓风拉拉一样，预计大岛将首当其冲地受到莫克降雨和强风的影响，因为它从周六晚间到周日早些时候直接袭击以南。
火奴鲁鲁国家气象局气象学家凯西·奥斯旺特表示，预计莫克将在周二早些时候继续在岛屿附近向西移动。
奥斯万特说：“影响仍然会存在，特别是对大岛的迎风面和东南面，但影响可能比我们在拉拉身上看到的要有限一些。”
拉拉砍倒了树木，将建筑物从地基上冲走，损坏了道路和桥梁，并使道路被泥土和岩石覆盖。据报道，有一起风暴导致死亡。
2026 年 8 月 17 日星期一，夏威夷州纳阿勒胡飓风拉拉过后，Ka’u 汽车修理店被一片废墟包围。（Stephen Lam/《旧金山纪事报》，美联社）
奥斯万特说，预计大岛东南部和迎风面的周末降雨量为 5 至 10 英寸（13 至 25 厘米），偏远地区可达 15 英寸（38 厘米）。岛链其他地区预计降雨量为 1 至 2 英寸（2 至 5 厘米），但毛伊岛东部部分地区降雨量可能高达 4 英寸（10 厘米）。
目前没有有效的沿海监视或警告，但敦促人们密切监视风暴的进展。该中心表示，降雨有可能引发危险的离岸流、危及生命的洪水和泥石流，特别是在陡峭地区和地面仍然饱和的地方。
据气象部门称，大岛东北海岸的拉拉总降雨量最大，达 43.54 英寸（1.1 米）。据 poweroutage.us 称，夏威夷大岛仍有 8,000 多名客户断电。
2026 年 8 月 16 日星期日，在夏威夷山景城，恶劣天气系统袭击该地区后，一名青少年涉水穿过受损道路被冲毁的水池。（斯蒂芬·林 / 旧金山纪事报，美联社）
夏威夷州州长乔什·格林和其他州官员在莫克之前举行了新闻发布会，敦促人们做好准备，补充食品、药品和其他必需品。
住在大岛东侧凯奥的教师蒂芙尼·爱德华兹·亨特 (Tiffany Edwards Hunt) 表示，一想到社区里的降雨量增多，洪水变成了河流，“空气中肯定弥漫着紧张气氛”。
美联社底特律撰稿人亚历克斯·圣约翰对此作出了贡献。

item.title: 随着谈判破裂和指责蔓延，美国和加拿大因新关税而陷入更深的贸易战
item.description:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States and Canada,historic alliesalong an undefended border, fell deeper into a trade war Saturday marked by angry recriminations and new tariffs that are expected to raise prices for products in both countries.
Each side blamed the other for the collapse of negotiations in Washington late Friday, leading the U.S. to impose 50% tariffs on$20 billion worth of Canadian goodsand Canada setting Sept. 8 as the start of its retaliatory penalties.
President Donald Trump’s import taxes will hit about 5% of whatCanada ships to the United Statesevery year, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Prime Minister Carney said Ottawa would respond with targeted tariff protection for industries exposed to the new U.S. duties, including some steel products. He also mentioned the dairy, appliance, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics sectors.
No further talks were planned. Whatever the eventual outcome, a loss of trust seems one of the earliest casualties.
Carney accused Washington of using “economic integration as a weapon” and said “its signature was written in pencil.” Resorting to the language of battle, he said his country had been “attacked” by the new American tariffs. “You’re at war when you get attacked,” he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond.
Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks about Canada’s response to new U.S. tariffs during a news conference on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Saturday, Aug. 22, 2026. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press via AP)
But to Trump’s chief trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, the U.S. was compelled to act after a year of retaliation by its longtime partner.
“We’ve said enough, and so we’ve taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains,” the U.S. trade representative told “Fox & Friends Weekend.”
Carney said Canada had been willing to drop remaining retaliatory tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos if the U.S. substantially lowered its own, and to encourage provinces to restore U.S. alcohol sales. But he said Washington’s final demands went too far. “They asked too much and offered too little,” Carney said.

Greer said the Republican administration was offering to cut tariffs on steel, autos and lumber, “things that are sensitive for them. And they’ve always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that.”
Rolled coils of steel sit in the yard at the ArcelorMittal Dofasco steel plant in Hamilton, Ont. on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Nick Iwanyshyn /The Canadian Press via AP)
As a result, he said, “We’re moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation.”
Carney said the U.S. added last-minute terms that would have reduced tariff relief for Canadian-made vehicles, restricted Canada’s ability to strike trade deals with other countries and weakened protections for language, culture and sovereignty.
He said such demands were “unacceptable.”
The breakdown in negotiations marked a sharp reversal from two days earlier, when officials from the two countries sounded as if they were headed toward a compromise.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who leads Canada’s most populous province, praised Carney for rejecting the deal, saying it would have hurt Ontario’s auto, steel and manufacturing sectors. Ford urged Canada to use “every tool in our toolbox” to fight the U.S. tariffs.
The moves also call into question the future of aNorth American trade agreementcovering the United States, Canada and Mexico that is crucial to industry in all three countries.
Carney said the breakdown was “certainly not good news” for the review of that agreement and that the failed negotiations had given Canada “a new perspective” on what Washington wants from the broader economic relationship.
The political impact will likely be even bigger than the economic fallout. The countries sold each other $880 billion worth of goods and services last year.
The tariffs were initially supposed to kick in at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday. Trump extended the deadline for three days to allow talks to continue, but the countries could not reach an agreement in time.
The U.S. and Canada have wrangled for decades over trade, poking each other over sore spots such as Canadian softwood lumber imports and U.S. access to Canada’s protected dairy market.
Somehow, they still managed to remain friends, allies and trading partners. Canadian soldiers fought alongside Americans in Afghanistan after 9/11. The 5,525-mile U.S.-Canada border is undefended, andnearly 330,000 peopleand $2 billion worth of goods cross it every day; 800,000 Canadians live in the United States.
Trump’s approach to dealing with Canada marks an extraordinary departure from the traditionally cooperative relationship between the two countries. Trump has imposed tariffs on Canadian goods in a push to bring manufacturing back to the United States and made inflammatory comments aboutturning Canada into America’s 51st state.
Carney said Canada had recognized that “America has changed” and that the two countries would “not return to our old relationship.”
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and chief trade negotiator Janice Charette listen as Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks about Canada’s response to new U.S. tariffs during a news conference on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Saturday, Aug. 22, 2026. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press via AP)
The Canadian public is fed up. A petition to expel U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, a Trump ally, has collected nearly 248,000 signatures since July 21. It accuses the former Republican congressman from Michigan of having “normalized’’ Trump’s talk of annexing Canada, among other things.
The two countries had good reasons to find a compromise.
Nearly72% of Canada’s goodsexports last year went to the United States. The Trump administration might be wary of imposing new tariffs — paid by U.S. importers who try to pass along the cost to consumers via higher prices — before the November midterm elections. American voters are already frustrated with the high cost of living.
“Both sides will be under immense pressure in the coming days to still find an off-ramp,” said Ryan Majerus, a partner at King & Spalding and a former U.S. trade official.
Joshua Bolten, CEO of the Business Roundtable, which represents leaders of major U.S. companies, warned the tariffs and retaliation risk “raising costs for American businesses and families” and disrupting vital supply chains, and urged both governments to resume negotiations.
Trump has made tariffs the centerpiece of his second-term economic agenda. Last year, he imposed double-digit import taxes on almost every country, justifying them by declaring the long-standing U.S. trade deficit a national emergency. The Supreme Court in February ruled that he had overstepped his authority. The justices struck down the trade penalties and set the stage for the federal government topay refunds to importers.
So Trump has looked for other legal authority to justify tariffs.
After the Supreme Court struck down much of Trump’s earlier tariff program in February, the administration turned to other legal authorities. For Canada, Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a rarely used Depression-era provision allowing tariffs of up to 50% against countries deemed to discriminate against U.S. businesses.
The provision is part of the Smoot-Hawley tariff law, widely blamed by economists and historians for worsening the Great Depression by restricting global trade. Section 338 has never previously been used to impose tariffs.
The rift comes as the United States, Mexico and Canada are trying to renew a trade agreement that Trump negotiated in his first term and once praised as a triumph. The United States has begun formal talks with Mexico over revamping the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, known as USMCA. But talks with Canada have not begun and escalating trade conflict casts doubt on whether they will.
Gillies reported from Toronto. Associated Press writer Michelle L. Price contributed to this report.

item.title: 特朗普翻修的白宫玫瑰园内部。首先是石头庭院，然后是雕像
item.description:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Instead of adding new roses, President Donald Trump’sWhite House Rose Gardenis growing statues.
Trump put statues of some of America’s founders in the garden just off the Oval Office after he replaced its plush lawn with awhite stone patio, turning the historic outdoor space into a look-alike of the one at his Mar-a-Lago home and private club in Palm Beach, Florida.
At least one statue was a gift. Others are on loan from people who wish to remain anonymous.
A statue of Alexander Hamilton is seen in the Rose Garden at the White House, March 6, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson, File)
The latest addition, a bronze depiction of a seated Thomas Jefferson signing the Declaration of Independence, was a gift from George Lundeen, a sculptor from Loveland, Colorado. It joins statues already displayed there of George Washington, Alexander Hamilton and Ben Franklin. A fifth sculpture named “Freedom’s Charge” is also on the patio.
The statues are part of Trump’s sweeping series ofWhite House renovations, from his gilded makeover of the Oval Office to theballroomandhelipadthat theRepublican presidentis having built on the south grounds. These projects fit into Trump’s broader plan to leave hismark on downtown Washingtonthrough otherconstruction projects, including astatue garden on federal landnear the National Mall.
Lundeen said he made the sculpture of Jefferson, the third U.S. president, decades ago and kept it at his ranch until he decided to spruce it up and send it to Trump for display at the White House in time for July Fourth celebrations ofAmerica’s 250th birthday. Steven Barber, his friend and collaborator, had reached out to contacts at the White House on Lundeen’s behalf.
“I thought it would just be a real nice thing on the 250th for people to look at Thomas Jefferson as he was writing the Declaration of Independence,” Lundeen said in a telephone interview.
But the statue did not get to the White House in time. Barber said it was stuck on a truck partly because of heavy security around the celebratory events. Trump was shown photos and liked the sculpture so much that he decided to put it in the Rose Garden.
When the president called Lundeen to thank him, he got voicemail. After the holiday, Lundeen’s office manager insisted he listen to one message in particular.

“Hi, George. It’s your favorite president, Donald Trump, and I just wanted to thank you,” the president said on the recording, which Lundeen shared with The Associated Press. “The sculpture, it looks really beautiful ... just by the picture I can see it’s really incredible, and we have a wonderful place right in the Rose Garden, and I appreciate it.”
Barber said in a separate telephone interview that he had been calling the White House for months to discuss the statue but got little in the way of a response until about three weeks before Independence Day, when in came a “flurry of emails saying they wanted it.”
A bronze statue of President George Washington is seen at the edge of the Rose Garden at the White House in Washington, Oct. 12, 2025. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein, File)
Details on the other statues added to the Rose Garden are relatively sparse.
The statue of Washington, America’s first president, was lent by Harlan Crow, the White House said. Representatives for the Texas-based real estate tycoon and GOP megadonor, who made headlines in recent years for hisfriendship with Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas, did not respond to email messages from the AP seeking comment.
A third statue, “Freedom’s Charge,” a 14-foot-tall (4.3-meter-tall) bronze sculpture of two Revolutionary War soldiers separated by a flag, was relocated from Dallas. Chas Fagan, the sculptor, did not respond to emailed requests for comment.
The Franklin and Hamilton statues are from anonymous donors, according to the White House.
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle explained Trump’s fondness for statues by saying that no other president has done more to beautify the White House and its surroundings.
“From restoring our treasured landmarks, which had suffered years of abuse and vandalism, to cleaning our parks and the Reflecting Pool, President Trump’s bold vision ensured that America rang in its 250th birthday celebration with glory and pride,” Ingle said in an emailed statement that referenced Trump’s troubled effort to spruce upthe pool near the Lincoln Memorial.
He said Trump continues to make “long-overdue and necessary” renovations to the White House.
“Thanks to the Builder-in-Chief, the White House will be properly glorified and remain in excellent condition for generations to come,” Ingle said.
President Donald Trump walks on the red carpet in the Rose Garden with Britain’s King Charles III, Queen Camilla and first lady Melania Trump at the White House, April 28, 2026, in Washington, during a State Visit. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon, File)
Next door to the White House, Trump had astatue of Christopher Columbus installedon the grounds of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in March.
More recently, the National Park Service installed a series of sculptures of Revolutionary-era subjects and themes at a plaza near the White House.
Trump’s marquee statue plan involves building aNational Garden of American Heroesnear the National Mall that would feature sculptures of 250 Americans who have made significant cultural, political and other historical contributions to the United States. Several preservation and cultural heritage organization have sued to block the project, arguing that Congress must first authorize it.
Barber said he and Lundeen are “in the mix” to make statues for that garden, too.
At his golf club in West Palm Beach, Florida, Trump has on display a 7-foot (2.1-meter) bronze sculpture depicting him with his fist raised after the 2024 assassination attempt during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. It was also made by Lundeen and was given to Trump by Anthony Constantino, a businessman and Republican congressional candidate from New York.
A statue of Ben Franklin is seen as servers prepare the Rose Garden for a dinner after President Donald Trump hosted the 2026 College Football Playoff national champions Indiana University on the South Lawn of the White House, May 11, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin, File)
The White House has long been a showcase for art, perhaps no work more famous than the Gilbert Stuart portrait of Washington that hangs in the East Room and was saved by first lady Dolly Madison after the British set the White House on fire during the War of 1812.
Presidents have access to the White House’s vast art collection. Trump has said he went to the “vaults” and found the presidential portraits and other art he hung in the Oval Office and in other rooms in the White House. Portraits of former presidents and former first ladies also adorn hallways and public rooms in the mansion.
In Trump’s first term, first lady Melania Trump installeda piece by Japanese American sculptor Isamu Noguchinear the Rose Garden, making him the first Asian American artist to be featured in the White House collection.
Before that, then-first lady Michelle Obama’s renovation of the Old Family Dining Room in 2015 included the addition of a painting by Alma Thomas, who was the first African American female artist to have her work added to the collection.

item.title: 特朗普敦促法院驳回BBC在诽谤案中获取其家人记录的请求
item.description:
华盛顿（美联社）——唐纳德·特朗普总统敦促联邦法官驳回 BBC 请求法院帮助获取三名家庭成员的证词和文件的请求，以回应他针对英国广播公司提起的价值 100 亿美元的诽谤诉讼。
这位共和党总统的私人律师在周五的法庭文件中辩称，BBC 正试图通过向女儿伊万卡·特朗普、女婿贾里德·库什纳和儿子小唐纳德·特朗普发出传票来获得对特朗普的“政治影响力”。
迈阿密的美国地区法官杰弗里·昆茨没有立即对这一纠纷做出裁决。
被特朗普提名为法官的昆茨不到一周前从另一位法官手中继承了总统的诉讼。法院文件没有立即具体说明案件重新分配的原因。前任法官已定下二月的审判日期。
据总统的律师称，今年 5 月，一名为 BBC 工作的传票员试图在伊万卡·特朗普和库什纳的住所向他们送达传票，但遇到了特勤局特工，特勤局特工表示他们无权接受传票。他们表示，几天后，流程服务器还访问了纽约的特朗普大厦，但未能为小唐纳德·特朗普提供服务。
在上周提交的法庭文件中，该广播公司请求法院允许通过挂号信而不是亲自向特朗普的家人送达传票。
特朗普于 12 月提起诉讼，指控 BBC 对他 2021 年 1 月 6 日在白宫附近发表的演讲的部分内容进行了欺骗性编辑，当时特朗普的一群支持者袭击了国会大厦，以阻止国会认可民主党人乔·拜登战胜特朗普。该诉讼称，BBC 将特朗普演讲的不同部分拼接在一起，故意歪曲他的言论。
该诉讼称，BBC 在 2024 年总统大选前一周播出了这部纪录片，“公然试图干涉和影响”选举结果，损害特朗普的利益。
特朗普的律师写道：“BBC 动议所寻求的救济不能与该动议所基于的充满政治色彩的发现运动分开，而该运动已被本法院裁定为不当过于宽泛。”

item.title: 2025 年事件重播中，在芝加哥和洛杉矶举行的 WNBA 比赛因被扔到球场上的性玩具而中断
item.description:
周五晚上，芝加哥天空队主场对阵金州勇士队的比赛因多个性玩具被扔到球场上而被中断，这是连续第二个晚上出现类似于上赛季几场 WNBA 比赛中发生的情况。
事件发生在天空队73-70战胜女武神队的第三节。球员们留在球场上，而球馆工作人员则将物品从球场上移走。
据《纽约时报》报道，亚特兰大周四以 124-88 战胜洛杉矶火花队的比赛也因同样原因而推迟。洛杉矶警方表示，一名男性嫌疑人被球馆保安拘留，收到传票后被释放。
上赛季亚特兰大、纽约和洛杉矶也发生过类似事件。其中一些事件导致被捕。

item.title: 跨性别辩论在 Fever 比赛中引发集会，布里安娜·斯图尔特 (Breanna Stewart) 希望有一个安全的空间
item.description:
纽约（美联社）——纽约自由队球星布里安娜·斯图尔特一直将 WNBA 视为一个包容性的地方，为球迷和球员提供安全的空间。最近这一点受到了挑战。
最近，WNBA 一直是关于是否应该允许跨性别女性（出生时被指定为男性，但为了适应自己的性别认同而转变）的辩论的主题。WNBA从来没有出现过这样的球员。尽管联盟的集体谈判协议规定 WNBA 仅限女性参加，但它没有包含有关性别认同或出生性别的更具体的语言。
印第安纳狂热队的索菲·坎宁安 (Sophie Cunningham) 在上个月发布的 ESPN 简介中表示，她反对变性女孩和妇女参加女子和女子运动项目，此后，印第安纳狂热队的索菲·坎宁安 (Sophie Cunningham) 表示，她反对跨性别女孩和妇女参加女子和女子运动项目，这一问题达到了紧要关头，随后，印第安纳狂热队比赛场外出现了小型集会和抗议活动。在周六晚上狂热队对阵纽约自由队之前，举行了两次代表跨性别问题双方的和平集会。
周六上午，斯图尔特对一小​​群记者表示：“知道双方都在举行集会，这表明W党拥有的平台和吸引注意力的噱头只是在继续尝试驾驭我们现有的浪潮。”“我希望今晚来到这里的自由球迷甚至印地球迷能够让这个竞技场成为一个安全的空间。”
坎宁安认为，她的评论所吸引的所有关注都是积极的，因为它为比赛带来了更多粉丝。
“你有很多新球迷，他们不仅会观看比赛，还会来看比赛，看看环境，看看人才，”她在赛前说道。“我认为任何时候你都能吸引更多人关注 W，这是一件很棒的事情，因为这会激励其他可能从未见过这款游戏、听说过这款游戏或参加过游戏的孩子，他们会获得这种体验。所以我绝对认为这是一件非常积极的事情。”
上周日在亚特兰大梦想队和狂热队之间的比赛中，至少三名球迷被 WNBA 安保人员要求遮盖印有变性女性参与女子运动的信息的衬衫。联盟后来表示球迷应该可以自由穿着这些球衣。
斯图尔特特别表示，自由球迷和 WNBA 球迷都会来观看比赛，因为“他们会觉得自己可以以任何身份做自己，我们不想忽视这一点。”
这位自由前锋表示，每个人都有权发表自己的意见，如果这种情况不再被允许，就会出现更大的问题。然而，她表示，不应容忍试图分裂球队和球员的行为。
“如果我们不允许（言论自由），我们需要真正回去看看更多的事情。我认为更重要的是人们试图将我们划分为团队、队友或对手，”她说。“这个联盟具有令人难以置信的包容性，也是我们继续争取和反对的目标。因此，我们不想剥夺这个平台。”
斯图尔特在她的职业生涯中一直是跨性别群体的盟友。去年，当她的一款签名鞋带有哈利波特主题时，她在网上遭到了一些强烈反对。斯图尔特是《哈利·波特》系列书籍和作者 J.K. 所著后续电影的忠实粉丝。罗琳斯因其反变性而受到批评。
斯图尔特已将该鞋的版税捐赠给了 Trevor Project，这是一个针对 LGBTQ+ 青少年的自杀预防和危机干预非营利组织。

item.title: D后卫主教练托里·洛武洛表示，在科特尔·马尔特神秘失踪后，他感到“被背叛”
item.description:
菲尼克斯（美联社）——亚利桑那响尾蛇队正处于一场激烈的季后赛争夺之中，截至周五还剩 34 场比赛，他们试图排除干扰，打出最好的棒球成绩，努力自 2023 年以来首次重返季后赛。
科特尔·马尔特（Ketel Marte）使这基本上成为不可能。
这位三届全明星球员在波士顿的客场之旅中神秘失踪四天后，在他们最好的球员之一在赛季的关键时刻实质上迷惑了队友和管理层之后，D后卫们仍在试图弄清楚如何继续前进。
“当我看到正在发生的事情时，我变得非常沮丧，”经理托里·洛武洛说。“我感到被背叛了。那是一种完全不同类型的痛苦和挫败感。但我已经克服了。”
洛武洛表示，他周四会见了马尔特，以及总经理迈克·哈森和马尔特的经纪人。这位32岁的二垒手在比赛结束后不久就因左膝发炎而被列入10天伤病名单。
洛武洛没有透露讨论的很多细节，但他确实表示，马特对他生病的膝盖感到有些沮丧。这位替补击球手原定在周一晚上缺席比赛之前成为球队的指定击球手。
马特本赛季打出 0.249 的本垒打，打出 21 个本垒打，打点 67 个，但在周五接受媒体采访时他并未出现在俱乐部会所。
“处理事情的方法有正确的，也有错误的，”洛武洛说。“我认为昨天得出的结论是我们本可以做得更好。具体来说，科特尔本可以做得更好。诚然如此。
“我想管理棒球比赛。我想做我喜欢在白线之间做的事情，而不必回答这些类型的问题。......我不喜欢这个球俱乐部之后的戏剧。我想成为一支优秀的棒球队，我们必须解决这个问题。”
后卫们可能更愿意应对马尔特令人困惑的行为，因为他目前是球队任职时间最长的球员，也是球队历史上最有生产力的击球手之一。自2017年加入俱乐部以来，多米尼加人共击出1,215支安打和189支本垒打，在俱乐部中广受好评。他的合同到2030年为止，并拥有2031年的球员选项。
“我爱科特尔·马尔特——我和他的关系不会改变，”洛武洛说。
但毫无疑问，反复无常的马尔特让球队陷入了困境。
这并不是他第一次发生奇怪的失踪事件。
上个赛季，他在亚利桑那州的家在全明星周末期间被闯入，因此被列入限制名单。他飞回祖国多米尼加共和国后缺席了三场比赛，后来为缺席表示歉意。
对于马尔特最近的缺席，很多队友都表示不太了解情况，主要是看媒体报道来了解详情。
救援人员凯文·金克尔（Kevin Ginkel）表示，情况令人失望，但他也关心马尔特，并希望他在精神和身体上都保持健康。
“这真的没有解释，”金克尔说。“但是我们还剩下 30 多场比赛，希望我们能让他回来，这会给我们进入季后赛带来很大的推动。”
金克尔说，队友们都渴望了解马特的故事。目前还不清楚这种情况何时或是否会发生。
“我认为听到这个消息会很高兴——当然，”金克尔说。“我认为很多球员对这件事的发生感到有点沮丧。但最重要的是，他的膝盖要恢复正常，并且精神上处于良好的状态，以便他可以回来帮助做出贡献。”

item.title: 摩城早期歌曲作家珍妮·布拉德福德·霍布斯 (Janie Bradford Hobbs) 因病在洛杉矶去世，享年 87 岁
item.description:
摩城早期歌曲作家珍妮·布拉德福德·霍布斯 (Janie Bradford Hobbs) 的家人周六表示，她因长期患病在洛杉矶一家医院去世，她曾帮助创作了《Money (That's What I Want)》和《Too Busy Thinking About My Baby》等热门歌曲。她87岁了。
布拉德福德·霍布斯出生于密苏里州查尔斯顿，后来搬到底特律。
20 世纪 50 年代末，她经邻居兼歌手杰基·威尔逊 (Jackie Wilson) 介绍认识了摩城创始人贝里·戈迪 (Berry Gordy)。她于 1958 年加入摩城担任接待员，与公司的许多员工一样，她参与了创意过程，帮助摩城成为音乐行业的巨头。
她和戈迪合写了《金钱（这就是我想要的）》。这首歌由 Barrett Strong 于 1959 年录制，并成为早期热门歌曲。它被披头士乐队翻唱，也成为该乐队的热门歌曲之一。
《Too Busy Thinking About My Baby》首先由 The Temptations 录制，后来成为马文·盖伊 (Marvin Gaye) 的热门歌曲。布拉德福德·霍布斯还为史蒂夫·旺德、The Supremes、Martha & The Vandellas 等人创作了歌曲。
戈迪在一份声明中说：“珍妮从一开始就和我在一起，甚至在摩城还没有出现之前，她将永远在我心中和摩城大家庭中占据一个非常特殊的位置。”
“珍妮是我一直认为摩城家族的特殊群体之一，他们是无名英雄，在人们知道摩城会变成什么样子之前，他们就相信了自己的梦想，”戈迪继续说道。“她是帮助摩城发展成为现在这个样子的人之一。”
布拉德福德·霍布斯后来成为摩城出版公司乔贝特的作家关系主管。离开摩城后，她创办了年度英雄与传奇奖。据她的家人称，这项活动持续了大约 30 年，旨在表彰音乐偶像并颁发奖学金。
她的丈夫沃丁·霍布斯（Wardean Hobbs）去世了。女儿，妮可·霍布斯；儿子兰斯·芬尼；和两个孙子。葬礼尚未完成。

item.title: 秋季书籍：期中销售季期间，小说成为书店的焦点
item.description:
NEW YORK (AP) —Midterm electionnews will fill the headlines this fall, but, among book buyers, fiction will likely have top billing.
Former PresidentJoe Biden’s“Promise Me, America” stands out not just as a White House memoir — presidential memoirs are events unto themselves — but as a rare high-profile political book over the next few months. Nonfiction sales have slumped in recent years and political books haven’t approached the peaks ofPresident Donald Trump’sfirst term.
“The energy in political books seems to be subdued. I think folks are just ranted out,” says Kristen McLean, an analyst and vice president for client insights at Circana, which tracks retail book sales.
“I think the (news) cycle is moving a bit too quickly for a lot of the very specific political books to catch on,” says Shannon DeVito, Barnes & Noble’s senior director of books.
Michael Lewis’ “Blockers,” a probe into Trump’s second term through the eyes of government workers, may be the only new release to rival the impact of Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s summer bestseller,“Regime Change.”This fall’s notable political offerings otherwise revisit the Biden years, from “Promise Me, America,” to former Middle East envoy Brett McGurk’s “Brink: Inside the Race to Free the Oct. 7 Hostages” to Akbar Shahid Ahmed’s study of Biden’s Gaza war policies, “Crossing the Red Line.”
Even Bob Woodward, who for decades released timely exposés of sitting presidents, is passing on current politics. In “Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir,” he reflects on presidents and White House sources dating back to the Nixon administration and the Watergate scandal that made him famous..
“Because he’s going more into his own life, I expect he’ll have a different and broader audience than for his other books,” DeVito says.
Novelists Barbara Kingsolver and Hernan Diaz, co-winners three years agoof the Pulitzer Prize, will share honors again as two of the featured authors in a busy season.Kingsolver’s “Partita,”about a onetime musical prodigy drawn again to her past, is the first since “Demon Copperhead,” her Pulitzer-winning retelling of Charles Dickens’ “David Copperfield.” Meanwhile, Diaz has followed his Pulitzer-winning “Trust” with thedystopian, Dickensian “Ply,”about a young thief in a chaotic future society.
Diaz says he met Kingsolver at the Pulitzer ceremony, where the two drank bourbon and bonded over literature and other common interests.
“I don’t think literature is a race or a tennis tournament,” Diaz says. “I think the more good books that are out there, the richer the conversation becomes and the more readers are engaged.”
Fiction sales have been solid in 2026 and will likely remain high if only because the two most prominent romantasy authors,Rebecca YarrosandSarah J. Maas, have new books coming. Maas is releasing “A Court of Splintered Harmony,” the sixth volume of “A Court of Thorns and Roses,” with the seventh installment scheduled for early next year. Yarros’ “Threshing Day” compiles 13 stories featuring characters from her Empyrean series, and her stand-alone “Peculiar Stars” finds protagonist Callista Moran stranded on an island after a sailing accident and discovering unexpected sides to herself.
The new fiction list also features Nobel laureate Jon Fosse’s latest, “Vaim Hotel,” and three contenders for theBooker Prize— Marlon James’ “The Disappearers,” Emma Cline’s “Switzy” and Rebecca Perry’s “May We Feed the King.” The book most primed for gossip is Rachel Cusk’s “Life of M,” a meta-novel about a movie star who may or may not be based onNatalie Portman.The season’s longest-awaited novel is likely Chad Harbach’s “The Brightness”: The parallel and intertwining lives of two close friends in their 20s is his first novel since his acclaimed 2011 debut, “The Art of Fielding.”
Min Jin Lee’s “American Hagwon” is her first novel since 2017 and her celebrated “Pachinko.” Emily St. John Mandel’s “Exit Party” is a story of futuristic breakdown from the author of the futuristic classic “Station Eleven.” Yiyun Li, Edwidge Danticat, Kate Atkinson, Deesha Philyaw, Diane Williams, Laleh Khadivi, R.F. Kuang and Norah Labiner also have fiction coming out.
Fans ofStephen King(and the late Peter Straub) can look forward to “Other Worlds Than These,” the final “Talisman” novel. Alice Hoffman launches a new series with “The Witches of Cambridge” and Brandon Sanderson has begun “Blightfall,” written with Janci Patterson. “The French Illusion” isJohn Grisham’slatest thriller. S.A. Cosby’s “Truth to Power” is a Marvel Crime novel featuring superhero/sleuth Luke Cage.
A selection of covers of celebrity memoirs releasing in fall 2026. (Random House/Gallery Books/Simon Six/The Open Field/Grand Central Publishing/Knopf/Harper/Dey Street/Legacy Lit/William Morrow via AP)
A trio of Oscar-winning superstars will tell their stories this fall:Sylvester Stallone’s“The Steps,” its title a reference to the actor’s iconic upward run in “Rocky”;Michael Douglas’“One Helluva Ride,” which the actor and producer has called a corrective to the blurry legends of fame; andDustin Hoffman’s“Look at Me,” promoted by publisher Simon Six as “an intimate memoir about art, ambition, family, friendship, love, aging, and the mysteries of a creative life.”
Gloria Steinemlooks back on her early years in “An Unexpected Life” and former NFL quarterbackColin Kaepernickreflects on his activism in “The Perilous Fight.” Chuck Lorre’s “Sitcom” is a memoir from the creator behind “Two and a Half Men” and “The Big Bang Theory.”Eric Dane’s“My Book of Days” comes out just months after the“Grey’s Anatomy” star diedfrom ALS.
Ancient poetry seems new again thanks to Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of“The Odyssey,”which has placededitions by Emily Wilsonand the late Robert Fagles high on bestseller lists. Wilson has a new book out this fall, “Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea,” essays that cover everything from Greek tragedy to “slut-shaming” Helen of Troy to the “sly laughter” ofCardi BandMegan Thee Stallion’s“WAP.”
In “Cloud Runner,” former U.S. poet laureateJoy Harjotries to express what she acknowledges may be inexpressible, the death three years ago of her daughter, Rainy Ortiz: “I have lost my girl./Some things do not belong in words,” Harjo writes. Jennifer Franklin channels the mind of James Joyce’s gifted, ill-fated daughter Lucia in the collection “A Fire in Her Brain.”
New work is also expected from Layli Long Soldier, Tina Chang, Patricia Lockwood, Dalia Taha, Avis Blackbird and Hieu Minh Nguyen. The anthology “Other Legacies” features tributes from Rae Armantrout, Edward Hirsch and other prizewinners to such lesser-known poets as Rachel Loden, Julia de Burgos and Stephen Jonas.
Covers of poetry books releasing in fall 2026. (Princeton University Press/Penguin Books/W. W. Norton/Ecco/Graywolf Press/W. W. Norton/Wesleyan University Press/Graywolf Press via AP)
Another writer enriched by a Nolan movie — Kai Bird, co-author of “American Prometheus,” the biography adaptedinto “Oppenheimer”— has co-written “American Scoundrel,” the story of lawyer/political fixer/Trump mentor Roy Cohn. In “The Rush,” award winner Nathaniel Philbrick revisits the 19th century quest for gold. The acclaimed science writer James Gleick examines the evolution of communication in “The Telephone: A New History.”
Two books, Timothy W. Ryback’s “53 Days” and Victor Sebestyen’s “Weimar Germany,” examine the fall of democracy in 1930s Germany, while other releases warning of contemporary threats include Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s “End Times Fascism” and Pulitzer winner Jill Lepore’s “The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State.”
Public radio host Celeste Headlee’s “Freedom’s Daughters” is one of many works this fall that center on race and racism. Grandmaster Flash has collaborated with Robert “Scoop” Jackson on a history of rap and hip-hop, “Birth of a Culture,” and Stephanie Phillips’ music history “We Were Here” highlights artists from Sister Rosetta Tharpe to Living Colour.
Pulitzer winner Alan Taylor’s “Tower Hill” offers a fresh look at the 1831 rebellion led by the enslaved Nat Turner. In “Renaissance Men,” Harriet A. Washington honors three groundbreaking and overlooked Black physicians in a narrative spanning the mid-19th century to the mid-20th century, and resonating today.
